content: Urodynamic tests are utilized to evaluate individuals with urinary incontinence or other urinary symptoms, aiming to establish a definitive and objective diagnosis. These tests are invasive and time-consuming but are intended to guide the selection of the most effective treatment. The purpose of this review was to assess whether treatment based on a urodynamic diagnosis leads to better clinical outcomes compared to treatment guided solely by history and physical examination. The review also aimed to explore whether urodynamic investigations improve clinical outcomes, influence clinical decision-making, or if one type of urodynamic test is superior to another in managing incontinence. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Register, which includes trials from CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and other sources, up to February 19, 2013. They included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared clinical outcomes in individuals who underwent urodynamic testing versus those who did not, or trials comparing different types of urodynamic tests. Trials that did not report clinical outcomes were excluded. Eight trials involving approximately 1,100 participants were included, but data were available for only 1,036 women across seven trials. Of these, 526 women underwent urodynamic testing. There was some evidence of potential bias in the trials. For instance, one trial reported four unexplained deaths and 12 dropouts in the control group. The findings indicated that urodynamic tests significantly influenced clinical decision-making. Women in the urodynamic testing groups of three trials were more likely to have their management plans altered compared to the control groups (17% versus 3%, risk ratio [RR] 5.07, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.87 to 13.74). However, there was statistical heterogeneity in these results. Two trials showed that women who underwent urodynamic testing were more likely to receive medication (RR 2.09, 95% CI 1.32 to 3.31). However, in five trials, women who underwent urodynamic testing were not more likely to undergo surgery (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.12). Importantly, there was no statistically significant difference in the rates of urinary incontinence between women whose treatment was guided by urodynamic testing (37%) and those whose treatment was based on history and clinical findings alone (36%). For example, the risk ratio for incontinence after one year was 1.02 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.21). It was estimated that 100 women (95% CI 86 to 114) would need to undergo urodynamic testing to prevent one additional case of incontinence after one year. One trial reported adverse effects, but no significant difference was observed between the groups (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.50). In conclusion, while urodynamic tests influenced clinical decision-making, there was limited evidence that they improved outcomes in terms of urinary incontinence rates after treatment. There was no data on the use of urodynamic tests in men, children, or individuals with neurological conditions. Larger, well-designed trials are needed to determine whether urodynamic testing leads to higher continence rates compared to management based on history and clinical examination alone.
